# University College London (UCL) Summary
University College London (UCL), founded in 1826, is a leading multidisciplinary university based primarily in the Bloomsbury area of London, with a growing presence at the UCL East campus in Stratford. UCL is known for its liberal secular origins, its historic buildings such as the Wilkins Building and the Cruciform Building, and its emphasis on environmental sustainability with green initiatives like carbon neutrality and biodiversity targets. The university owns 26 halls of residence and guarantees accommodation to most first-year students. Its student life is vibrant, supported by an active Students' Union, more than 250 student societies, and numerous sports clubs.
Academically, UCL comprises eleven faculties offering research and teaching across a broad range of disciplines. It is highly selective, attracting international students who make up the majority of its student body since 2017. UCL is a major research institution, receiving over £538 million in research income annually, and partners with prestigious organizations like the Francis Crick Institute and the Alan Turing Institute. The university’s libraries contain over two million books and vast special collections, while its museums and collections—including the Petrie Museum and Grant Museum—support both research and teaching. UCL is consistently ranked among the top universities globally, regularly appearing in the top 25 of major rankings. It is a founding member of the Russell Group and part of the 'golden triangle' of top UK research universities. Notable for its impact on the UK economy and scholarly output, UCL has produced many prominent alumni and staff, including numerous Nobel laureates.
